title: Linear Data Structures: Linked Lists, Stacks, and Queues
description: Implementing singly linked lists, array-based and linked stacks, and array-based and circular queues in C.
objectives: Implement a singly linked list with insertion and traversal
Implement a stack using an array
Implement a queue, including a circular queue

content.heading: Singly Linked Lists
content.body:
A linked list is built from nodes, each a struct holding data and a pointer to the next node: struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; };. Unlike an array, a linked list's nodes need not be contiguous in memory — each is individually malloc()'d and linked via pointers, letting the list grow dynamically without a pre-declared fixed capacity, at the cost of losing O(1) indexed access (finding the i-th element requires walking i nodes from the head).

Inserting at the front requires updating the caller's head pointer itself, which (as covered in the Pointers lesson) requires a pointer to a pointer (struct Node **headRef) if done inside a separate function, since a plain struct Node *head parameter would only receive a local copy of the pointer.

content.heading: Stacks and Queues
content.body:
A stack (LIFO — last in, first out) can be implemented with a fixed-size array and a top index: push() increments top and writes the new value; pop() reads the value at top and decrements it — both should check for overflow (stack full) and underflow (stack empty) respectively before proceeding.

A queue (FIFO — first in, first out) can similarly use a fixed-size array with front and rear indices: enqueue() writes at rear and advances it; dequeue() reads at front and advances it — but a naive array-based queue 'wastes' the freed space at the front as elements are dequeued. A circular queue fixes this by wrapping the indices back to 0 using modulus arithmetic once they reach the array's end ((rear + 1) % capacity), reusing the freed slots and letting a fixed-size array support continuous enqueue/dequeue cycling without ever needing to shift elements.

content.explanation: insertFront uses a pointer-to-pointer to correctly update the caller's head. The circular queue's rear = (rear + 1) % CAP wraps the index back to 0 once it reaches the array's capacity, reusing freed slots.

keyPoints: A linked list's nodes are individually allocated and linked via pointers, allowing dynamic growth without a fixed capacity
Updating a linked list's head from inside a function requires a pointer to a pointer
An array-based stack uses a single top index; check for overflow/underflow before push/pop
A circular queue uses modulus arithmetic on its front/rear indices to reuse freed array slots
commonMistakes: Forgetting to check for stack overflow/underflow before push()/pop()
Implementing a naive (non-circular) array-based queue that wastes freed space at the front
Passing a plain pointer (not a pointer-to-pointer) to a function that needs to update the list's head
